title: Are Catholics and Protestants Both Christians?
excerpt: Catholics and Protestants confess the same creeds and divided in the sixteenth century over authority, justification, the sacraments, and Mary and the saints. Each side's teaching is given here in words its own teachers wrote, with what has changed since and what has not.
body:
A woman raised Catholic marries into a Protestant family, and at her first Thanksgiving with them an aunt asks, meaning it kindly, when she became a Christian. A man remembers being told in his church's youth group that Catholics pray to statues and trust their own good deeds, and he believed it until he sat with a Catholic friend whose mother was dying and heard what the friend actually prayed. An old man remembers the other half. As a boy he was taught that the Protestants across the road had left the one true church, and that the kindest thing he could do for them was pray they came back.

The skeptic watching has an obvious remark. These people recite the same creed, read nearly the same Bible, and spent a good part of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries killing each other. If they can't agree on who counts as one of them, why should he listen to either?

The question in the title is asked in both directions, and it deserves a plain answer before the details. Measured by the creeds that the whole church confessed before either name existed, yes. What divides them is real, some of it is grave, and it is not at that level.

## What They Share

A Catholic and a Protestant who stand to say the Apostles' Creed say the same words. They confess one God, the Father almighty, and Jesus Christ his only Son, "born of the Virgin Mary," who "suffered under Pontius Pilate," rose on the third day, and will come to judge the living and the dead. With the creed of the fourth century both confess the Son to be of one substance with the Father. Both baptize in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Both read the same twenty-seven books as the New Testament, and both believe that a sinner is saved by the grace of God through the death and resurrection of Christ, and by nothing a human being could offer in its place.

That last point is so often denied in arguments between them that it should be shown and not just asserted. The Council of Trent, which gave Rome's formal answer to the Reformation, begins its canons on the subject with this: "If any one saith, that man may be justified before God by his own works, whether done through the teaching of human nature, or that of the law, without the grace of God through Jesus Christ; let him be anathema." Whatever else a Protestant believes about Catholic teaching, he may not say that it teaches people to earn heaven without grace. Its first canon on the matter rejects the idea.

So the Trinity, the incarnation, the cross, the bodily resurrection and the life to come are common ground. That is the floor on which this site stands, and it is stated here as confession. Everything that follows is a dispute among people who are standing on it.

## Who Has the Last Word

The Reformation began in 1517 over the sale of pardons, and within four years it had become an argument about authority, because that is where every other argument ended. When a teacher and the church disagree about what Scripture means, who decides?

Rome's answer was given at Trent in 1546. The truth of the gospel, the council said, is "contained in the written books, and the unwritten traditions" that came down from the apostles, and the church receives both "with an equal affection of piety, and reverence." The church that Christ founded on Peter, to whom he said, "on this rock I will build my church" (Matthew 16:18), is the guardian and interpreter of both. Catholics point out that the apostles themselves commanded this: "hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter" (2 Thessalonians 2:15). Paul calls the church, and not the book, "a pillar and buttress of the truth" (1 Timothy 3:15). It was the church, after all, that recognized which books belonged in the Bible. And they point to what happened next. Take away a living teacher with authority to settle a dispute, and every reader becomes his own final court. The Protestant movement divided within twelve years of its beginning and has gone on dividing, as the essay here on [why there are so many denominations](/writing/why-are-there-so-many-denominations) describes.

The Protestant answer is in the confessions the reformers wrote. The English articles of religion from the same century say that "Holy Scripture containeth all things necessary to salvation," so that nothing which cannot be proved from it may be required of anyone as an article of faith. The Westminster Confession of 1646 names the judge by which "all decrees of councils, opinions of ancient writers, doctrines of men, and private spirits, are to be examined": it "can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture." Protestants did not throw out tradition. They kept the creeds, quoted the church fathers constantly, and wrote long confessions of their own. Their claim was narrower. Scripture alone cannot err, and everything else can, including a council. The same English articles say that councils "may err, and sometimes have erred." They pointed to Jesus' words to the religious teachers of his day, "You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men" (Mark 7:8), and they asked how a church that could not be corrected by Scripture would ever be reformed when it went wrong. It had just needed reforming, as Trent's own decrees on discipline admitted.

Each side fears something that has in fact happened. The Catholic fears a Christianity with no one able to say what it teaches. The Protestant fears a church that has made itself the measure of the book it was given.

## How a Sinner Is Made Right with God

The second dispute is the one Luther cared about most, and the one where the two sides are both closer and further apart than their members usually know.

The Protestant confession is short. The Lutherans told the emperor at Augsburg in 1530 that people "cannot be justified before God by their own strength, merits, or works, but are freely justified" for Christ's sake, through faith. Paul had written, "one is justified by faith apart from works of the law" (Romans 3:28), and that God "justifies the ungodly" (Romans 4:5). To be justified, on this account, is to be declared righteous in God's court on the ground of what Christ did, which is credited to the believer and received by faith alone. Good works follow, and they must. Westminster says that the faith which alone justifies "is no dead faith, but worketh by love." But the works are fruit. They are no part of the ground on which a sinner stands before God, and so a believer may know now, today, that he is accepted.

Trent's teaching is fuller than the slogan Protestants often give for it. Justification, it says, "is not remission of sins merely, but also the sanctification and renewal of the inward man." God does not only pronounce a person righteous. He makes him so, by grace poured into him, and that grace can grow, can be lost by grave sin, and can be restored. Faith is "the beginning of human salvation, the foundation, and the root of all Justification," and it has to be joined by hope and love to be living faith. Catholics read Paul's phrase "faith working through love" (Galatians 5:6) as the whole matter in four words, and they point to a place where Scripture uses the very phrase "faith alone," where James writes that "a person is justified by works and not by faith alone" (James 2:24). Trent accordingly condemned the statement that "by faith alone the impious is justified," if that means nothing else is required.

What each side fears here is worth hearing. The Protestant fears that a person taught to look at the grace within him will never have peace, since what is within him is always mixed, and that he will end up trusting his own cooperation while calling it grace. The Catholic fears a pardon that leaves the pardoned man unchanged, a sentence of acquittal read over someone who has not changed, and a religion in which holiness becomes optional. Each also denies the charge. The Protestant insists that real faith always produces a changed life. The Catholic insists that every good work is itself God's gift.

## The Sacraments, Mary and the Saints

The third dispute is about how grace reaches people. Trent ruled that the sacraments are neither "more, or less, than seven": baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist, penance, anointing of the sick, ordination and marriage. The Protestant confessions count two, "ordained of Christ our Lord in the Gospel, that is to say, Baptism, and the Supper of the Lord," and regard the other five as good practices or states of life that Christ did not institute as sacraments.

The sharpest edge was the Mass. Trent taught that in it the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ in substance, and that the Mass is a real sacrifice, offered for the living and the dead. The reformers answered that Christ's offering was finished, "for by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified" (Hebrews 10:14). Catholics reply that the Mass is that same one offering made present and not a second one. Protestants then disagreed among themselves about what the Supper is, and the essay on [the Lord's Supper](/writing/what-is-the-lords-supper) sets out those five answers.

The fourth dispute is the one most visible from the pew. Trent taught that the saints "offer up their own prayers to God for men" and that "it is good and useful suppliantly to invoke them." Catholics distinguish this from worship, which belongs to God alone. Asking a saint to pray, they say, is no different in kind from asking a friend to pray, and Scripture commands that: "pray for one another" (James 5:16). Death does not cut a believer off from the body of Christ. The Lutheran confession honors the saints as examples and stops there: "the Scripture teaches not the invocation of saints," because "there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 2:5). Protestants add that no passage shows anyone praying to a departed believer, and that in practice the devotion often grows into something that looks very like worship whatever the catechism says.

On Mary the common ground is larger than either side tends to remember. Both confess that Jesus was born of a virgin. Both accept the title given her by the council of 451, the God-bearer, which was a statement about who her son is. Beyond that they part. Rome has since defined that she was conceived without sin (1854) and taken up body and soul into heaven (1950), and in 1870 it defined that the pope, under strict conditions, teaches without error. Protestants find none of the three in Scripture, and for them each new definition is the authority question asked again.

## The Orthodox, Who Were Not at the Quarrel

The Eastern Orthodox churches had been separated from Rome for more than four centuries when Luther was born. They stand with Rome on a good deal of this: seven sacraments, the honoring of Mary and the saints, and Scripture read within the church's tradition. A council of theirs at Jerusalem in 1672, answering Protestant ideas, said that the Scriptures are to be believed "yet not otherwise than as the Catholic Church has interpreted and delivered the same." They stand against Rome on the pope's authority over the whole church. And the Study Bible's study of justification notes that the Orthodox tend to see the Western fight over that doctrine as built on assumptions they never shared. Their presence is a reminder that this was always a family argument inside the Western half of the church.

## What We Did to Each Other

Neither side kept the dispute on paper. Trent attached a curse to each of its canons. Westminster, a century later, called the pope "that Antichrist, that man of sin and son of perdition." The catechism written at Heidelberg in 1563 called the Mass "an accursed idolatry." Then came the fire and the sword. Catholics burned Protestants, Protestants hanged priests, and both hunted the Anabaptists. From 1618 to 1648 a war that began over religion laid waste to central Europe. The history course here is blunt about the result. A continent learned to connect Christian conviction with killing, and a good deal of modern unbelief starts from that memory.

None of us can stand outside that. Protestants like to remember the stake and forget the gallows they built themselves. Catholics like to remember the martyred priests and forget who lit the fires. We did this to people who had been baptized into the same name and who said the same creed the morning they died.

## What Has Changed

Some things have. Trent itself reformed much of what Luther first protested; the history course records that the professional sellers of pardons were abolished and seminaries founded, and it says, "Rome did reform, and the reform was real." In 1964 the Second Vatican Council said of the division that "men of both sides were to blame," and that those born into Protestant churches who believe in Christ and are baptized "have a right to be called Christian," and are to be regarded "with respect and affection."

Other things have not changed, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. The definitions of 1854, 1870 and 1950 are additions since the Reformation, not subtractions. Protestants have not moved on Scripture as the only rule that cannot err.

## Are They Both Christians?

By the creeds, both are Christian churches, and a member of either who confesses the faith of those creeds is confessing the Christian faith. The disputes described here are of the second order: they divide faithful churches without dividing the faith. This essay takes no side in them.

That judgment has serious opponents on both sides, and their objection should be stated. There are Protestants who hold that justification by faith alone is the gospel itself, so that a church which condemns it has lost more than a secondary point. There are Catholics who hold that to be outside communion with the successor of Peter is to lack something Christ meant every believer to have. Neither objection is foolish, and this essay hasn't answered either in full. What can be said is that many who raise either objection also know someone on the other side whose trust in Christ they would not deny.

No church makes anyone a Christian by membership. Jesus warned that "not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 7:21), and that warning is read aloud in cathedrals and in storefront chapels to people who equally need it. He also told of a man who "went down to his house justified" (Luke 18:14), and all that man had said was, "God, be merciful to me, a sinner!" (Luke 18:13). That prayer is taught on both sides of the road.

The aunt at the Thanksgiving table and the old man who prayed for his neighbors' return were making the same mistake. Each had been taught the other's faith by people who did not hold it. On Sunday the two families will stand up a mile apart and say that they believe in one holy catholic and apostolic church. Both will mean it. Neither has yet found a way to say that sentence in the same room and then eat at the same table.

*"God, be merciful to me, a sinner!"* (Luke 18:13)

*"Is Christ divided?"* (1 Corinthians 1:13)
